readerTitle: The warehouse that gave out 12 awards and 1,250 thank-yous
caseNote: 가상 사례 (물류센터, B2B 마케팅 대행사) + 실제 연구 (Grant & Gino, 2010, 대학 기금 모금 콜센터)
insight: 인정은 상품이 아니라 정보다. 누가 무엇을 잘했는지 구체적으로, 자주 알려 줄 때 힘이 생기고, 상금의 크기는 그다음 문제다.
misconception: 인정하려면 돈이나 큰 상이 필요하다. 이달의 직원 상금을 올리면 모두가 더 열심히 일한다.

sources.text: Grant, A. M., & Gino, F. (2010). A little thanks goes a long way: Explaining why gratitude expressions motivate prosocial behavior. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 98(6), 946–955.
물류센터와 대행사 사례의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 물류센터 계산: 이달의 직원 상 $100 × 12개월 = 연 $1,200. 수상 12회 ÷ 40명 → 한 번도 중복 수상이 없어도 28명(40 − 12)은 1년 동안 아무것도 받지 못함. 고르게 돌아가도 1인당 약 3.3년에 한 번(40 ÷ 12).
구체적 감사 계산: 하루 5건 × 근무일 250일 = 연 1,250건. 1,250 ÷ 40명 = 1인당 연 약 31회. 250일 ÷ 31회 ≈ 8근무일마다 한 번. 하루 10분 × 250일 = 2,500분 ≈ 42시간(카드에는 'about 40 hours').

Grant & Gino(2010) 현장 연구: 대학 기금 모금 콜센터에서 연간 기부 담당 디렉터가 방문해 감사를 전한 그룹은 다음 주 통화 건수가 50% 이상 늘었고, 감사를 받지 않은 그룹은 변화가 없었다는 내용. 정확한 수치와 연구 번호(Study 4로 기억)를 원문에서 다시 확인하세요. 연구자들은 '사회적으로 가치 있게 여겨진다는 느낌'을 원인으로 제시함.

cards.title: The warehouse that gave out 12 awards and 1,250 thank-yous
body: A distribution center has 40 pickers. Every month, the manager names an Employee of the Month and hands over $100. That's $1,200 a year, and a photo on the wall.
The warehouse next door spends nothing on awards. Its people say they feel far more appreciated. The numbers explain why.

image.label: Warehouse wall with one employee photo, aisles full of workers
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일 물류센터. 벽에 'Employee of the Month' 액자 하나만 걸려 있고, 그 아래 선반 사이로 여러 명의 작업자가 상자를 옮기고 있음. 액자 속 인물만 밝게, 나머지는 살짝 흐리게. 실제 기업 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: You have $1,200 a year for recognition.
body: You run the 40-person warehouse. Morale is flat, and a supervisor suggests changing the Employee of the Month program.
What do you do with the budget?

options.text: Keep the award but make it quarterly, with a $300 prize
options.feedback: A bigger prize gets more attention, but now only 4 people a year are seen. The other 36 learn that their work goes unnoticed.

options.text: Drop the prize and spend 10 minutes a day thanking people for specific work
options.feedback: You trade one big moment for hundreds of small ones. It costs your time, not money, and nearly everyone hears that their work was seen.

options.text: Split it evenly: $30 for each person at year end
options.feedback: Fair and simple, but it says nothing about what anyone did. It reads as a small bonus, not as recognition.

cards.title: Count the moments, not the dollars.
body: Even if no one ever wins twice, **28 of 40 people** hear nothing all year. Five specific thank-yous a day reach each person about every eight working days.

breakdown.label: Times each person is seen
breakdown.detail: About 40 hours of the manager's time

cards.title: Recognition
body: **Recognition** is telling someone, clearly and soon, that you saw a specific piece of their work and that it mattered.
It is different from pay. Pay is a deal agreed in advance. Recognition is feedback after the fact: *I noticed what you did.* That is why small, frequent and specific beats big, rare and vague.

image.label: One large trophy versus many small speech bubbles
image.brief: 왼쪽에 큰 트로피 하나와 그 앞에 사람 한 명, 오른쪽에 작은 말풍선 여러 개가 여러 사람에게 각각 닿는 그림. 말풍선에는 'Fixed the label jam', 'Trained the new hire' 같은 짧은 문구. 오른쪽이 더 따뜻한 색감.

cards.title: A short thank-you changed how hard people worked.
body: Researchers Adam Grant and Francesca Gino studied fundraisers calling alumni for a university. One group got a brief visit from a director who said she was grateful for their work. Another group got no visit.

In the following week, the thanked group made **more than 50% more calls**. The other group's calls stayed flat. The researchers linked the effect to people feeling socially valued, not to any reward.

cards.title: Four things turn praise into recognition.
body: The thank-you only works if it carries real information.
list: **Specific:** name the action, not just "great job"
**Soon:** close to the moment, while it still matters
**Sincere:** from someone who actually saw it
**Effect:** say what it made possible for the team or customer
cards.callout: "Thanks for re-sorting aisle 9 before the 6 a.m. trucks. We loaded on time" beats any trophy.
cards.softwareNote: A #kudos channel full of "🙌 great work team" fades into noise. Thanking the engineer who fixed an unglamorous bug, and saying which customers stopped complaining, tells everyone what good work looks like.

cards.title: Recognition can't replace fair pay, and it can sour.
body: If people feel underpaid, warm words can read as a cheap substitute. Recognition sits on top of fair pay. It doesn't stand in for it.
Praise used as a tool also gets spotted fast. And not everyone likes the spotlight. For some, a quiet word beats a shout-out in front of the whole floor.

cards.title: Now it's a marketing agency.
body: Your account manager, Priya, stayed late to rebuild a client's broken campaign report before their board meeting. The client emails you: "Priya saved us."

options.text: Forward the email to the whole company with "Great job, Priya!"
options.feedback: It's quick and public. But it doesn't say what she did well, and some people dislike the spotlight more than they enjoy it.

options.text: Tell her today what you saw, what it meant for the client, and share their words
options.feedback: Specific, soon and tied to its effect. You can still share it with the team, framed around what she did so others learn from it.

options.text: Note it for her annual review to support a raise
options.feedback: It may help her pay later, which matters. But months of silence tell her nobody noticed tonight's effort.

cards.title: Recognition is a message, not a prize.
body: People need to hear, often and specifically, that their work was seen. Count how many people you reach, not how much you spend.
**Try it today:** before you leave, tell one person exactly what they did this week and what it made possible.
